CAP: A Connectivity-Aware Hierarchical Coverage Path Planning Algorithm for Unknown Environments using Coverage Guidance Graph

Zongyuan Shen    Burhanuddin Shirose    Prasanna Sriganesh    Matthew Travers ††thanks: All authors are from the Robotics Institute, Carnegie Mellon University, USA. {zongyuas, bshirose, pkettava, mtravers}@andrew.cmu.edu††thanks: Supplementary video - https://youtu.be/1pH-PkcRVZg
Abstract

Efficient coverage of unknown environments requires robots to adapt their paths in real time based on on-board sensor data. In this paper, we introduce CAP, a connectivity-aware hierarchical coverage path planning algorithm for efficient coverage of unknown environments. During online operation, CAP incrementally constructs a coverage guidance graph to capture essential information about the environment. Based on the updated graph, the hierarchical planner determines an efficient path to maximize global coverage efficiency and minimize local coverage time. The performance of CAP is evaluated and compared with five baseline algorithms through high-fidelity simulations as well as robot experiments. Our results show that CAP yields significant improvements in coverage time, path length, and path overlap ratio.

Index Terms:
Motion and Path Planning, Coverage Path Planning, Unknown Environments.

I Introduction

Optimized coverage path planning (CPP) enables robots to achieve complete coverage of all points in a search area efficiently. Existing CPP methods generate well-defined coverage patterns (e.g., the back-and-forth pattern shown in Fig. 1(a)) and ensure complete coverage in finite time, but prioritize immediate cost minimization, not considering a global perspective of the entire search area. These myopic decisions result in inefficient global coverage paths. Enabling efficient coverage requires reasoning about the topology of known and unknown parts of the environment and adapting the robot’s path as new information becomes available. To this end, we present a hierarchical coverage path planning algorithm that utilizes essential global information about the environment to efficiently guide the CPP process online.

To enable efficient coverage of unknown environments, we introduce CAP, a Connectivity-Aware Hierarchical Coverage Path Planning algorithm. CAP maintains and updates an environmental map online that makes it possible to dynamically identify disconnected subareas of an environment. The subareas are split into exploring (free-space adjacent to unknown regions) and explored (free-space fully mapped by the sensor, not adjacent to unknown regions) areas. CAP then incrementally constructs a coverage guidance graph by adding these subareas as new nodes with edges representing local connectivity between subareas, capturing the global topological structure of the environment. The graph is then used to compute an optimal subarea traversal tour by solving a traveling salesman problem (TSP). The TSP-based tour ensures that the robot follows a globally efficient sequence of subareas to explore. We find that this globally aware planner addresses issues of bypassing isolated regions and inefficient backtracking (Fig. 1). The coverage planner dynamically switches between a greedy strategy to initially cover the exploring subareas and a TSP-based optimal coverage plan within the explored subareas to further minimize local coverage time. CAP is illustrated in Fig. 2.

The specific contributions of this work are:

  • •

    Development of CAP for efficient coverage of unknown environments with two key components:

    • –

      Coverage guidance graph to capture essential environmental information for efficient planning.

    • –

      Hierarchical coverage path planning method to improve the global coverage efficiency and minimize local coverage time.

  • •

    Comprehensive comparison to baseline algorithms in simulation and real-world experiments.

II Related Work

Coverage path planning has been utilized in a variety of real-world robotic applications, such as seabed mapping, structural inspection, spray painting surfaces, floor cleaning, and aerial surveying [1, 2, 3]. CPP methods are broadly classified as offline or online [4]. Offline methods [5] rely on prior information of the environments to design coverage paths, which can be highly effective in ideal conditions. However, their performance degrades if the prior information is incomplete and/or incorrect. Therefore, it is essential to develop online CPP methods, which adapt the coverage path in real-time based on the collected environmental information.

Acar and Choset [6] developed a method which detects the critical points to decompose the area into multiple cells and incrementally constructs a Reeb graph that has edges as the cells and nodes as the critical points. Each cell is covered by certain coverage pattern. Gabriely and Rimon [7] developed the full spiral spanning tree covering algorithm to generate a spiral coverage path by following a spanning tree. Gonzalez et al. [8] presented the backtracking spiral algorithm (BSA), which generates a spiral path by following the uncovered area boundary and switches to a backtracking mechanism for escaping from the dead-end situation.

Luo and Yang [9] presented the biologically-inspired neural network (BINN) algorithm, which places a neuron at each grid cell. An activity landscape is updated such that the obstacle cells have negative potentials for collision avoidance and uncovered cells have positive potentials for coverage. Then, the target cell is selected in the local vicinity of robot using this activity landscape. Later in [10], this algorithm was improved to mitigate the dead-end situation. Viet et al. [11] presented the boustrophedon motions and A∗ (BA∗) algorithm, which performs back-and-forth motion until no uncovered cell is found in the local vicinity. Then, the robot moves to the backtracking cell to resume the coverage.

Song and Gupta [12] developed the ϵ∗\epsilon^{*} algorithm, which utilizes an exploratory Turing Machine as a supervisor to guide the robot online with tasking commands for coverage via back-and-forth motion. The algorithm uses multi-resolution adaptive potential surfaces to escape from a dead-end situation. Hassan and Liu [13] proposed the predator–prey CPP (PPCPP) algorithm, which determines target cell in the local vicinity of robot according to the immediate reward consisting of three components: 1) predation avoidance reward that maximizes the distance to the predator (predator is a user-defined stationary point), 2) smoothness reward that minimizes the turn angle, and 3) boundary reward for covering boundary of the uncovered area.

Some CPP methods have also been developed for 3D structure coverage [1, 2], multi-robot systems [14, 3], curvature-constrained robots [15, 16], tethered robots [17, 18], and energy-constrained robots [19, 20].

III CAP Algorithm

Let 𝒜⊂ℝ2\mathcal{A}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be the unknown area populated by obstacles. First, a tiling is constructed on 𝒜\mathcal{A} as defined below.

Definition III.1 (Tiling)

A set 𝒯={τj⊂ℝ2:j=1,…,|𝒯|}\mathcal{T}=\{\tau_{j}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}:j=1,\ldots,|\mathcal{T}|\} is a tiling of 𝒜\mathcal{A} if its elements 1) are mutually exclusive, i.e., τj∩τj′=∅,∀j,j′∈{1,…,|𝒯|},j≠j′\tau_{j}\cap\tau_{j^{\prime}}=\emptyset,\forall{j},{j^{\prime}}\in\{1,\ldots,|\mathcal{T}|\},{j}\neq{j^{\prime}}, and 2) cover 𝒜\mathcal{A}, i.e., 𝒜⊆⋃j=1|𝒯|τj\mathcal{A}\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{T}|}\tau_{j}.

It is recommended that the cell is big enough to contain the robot and small enough for the tasking device/sensor (e.g., cleaning brush) to completely cover it when the robot visits it. During online operation, the robot updates environmental information on 𝒯\mathcal{T} based on onboard sensor data and picks an uncovered free cell to cover. Thus, 𝒯\mathcal{T} is partitioned into three sets: 1) obstacle (𝒯o\mathcal{T}_{o}), 2) free (𝒯f\mathcal{T}_{f}), and 3) unknown (𝒯u\mathcal{T}_{u}). The free cells are further separated into two subsets: covered (𝒯fc\mathcal{T}_{f}^{c}) and uncovered (𝒯fu\mathcal{T}_{f}^{u}).

Let tc∈ℝ+t_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{+} be the time instant at which the environmental map is updated and the objective of CAP is to find an updated path σ:[tc,T]→𝒯f\sigma:[t_{c},T]\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{f} to provide complete coverage of 𝒜\mathcal{A} with minimized coverage time, where T∈ℝ+T\in\mathbb{R}^{+} is the total coverage time.

Definition III.2 (Complete Coverage)

Let τ⁡(t)∈𝒯f\tau(t)\in\mathcal{T}_{f} be the cell visited by the robot at time t∈[tc,T]t\in[t_{c},T]. Then, the coverage of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is said to be complete if ∃T∈ℝ+\exists T\in\mathbb{R}^{+}, s.t. the path σ≜[τ⁡(t)]t=tcT\sigma\triangleq[\tau(t)]_{t=t_{c}}^{T} covers 𝒯fu\mathcal{T}_{f}^{u}, i.e.,

𝒯fu⊆⋃t∈[tc,T]τ⁡(t)\mathcal{T}_{f}^{u}\subseteq\bigcup_{t\in[t_{c},T]}\tau(t) (1)

Therefore, we presents an algorithm consisting of three steps: 1) subarea identification, 2) coverage guidance graph construction, and 3) hierarchical coverage path planning.

III-A Identification of Disconnected Subareas

Definition III.3 (Exploring Area)

An uncovered free area is said to be exploring if it is adjacent to unknown area.

As seen in Fig. 2(a), the current area is an exploring area. Thus, the robot follows the greedy strategy by selecting an uncovered cell as target cell τt​a​r​g​e​t\tau_{target} in the local vicinity. This strategy could break the current area into multiple disconnected subareas that are surrounded by obstacles and covered area, as seen in Fig. 2(b).

Definition III.4 (Disconnected Subareas)

On tiling 𝒯\mathcal{T}, two subareas are said to be disconnected if there is no path connecting them by only traversing uncovered area 𝒯fu\mathcal{T}_{f}^{u}.

The process to find disconnected subareas is described as follows. First, an uncovered cell which does not belong to any identified subarea is picked in the local vicinity of robot and τt​a​r​g​e​t\tau_{target}, and assigned an index ℓ∈ℕ+\ell\in\mathbb{N}^{+}. Then, starting at this cell, the algorithm recursively searches and labels adjacent uncovered cells with the same index ℓ\ell in four directions (i.e., up, down, left, right) until no more adjacent uncovered cells can be found. These labeled cells are grouped together to form a subarea 𝒜ℓ\mathcal{A}_{\ell}. Its center position pℓp_{\ell} is computed as the average position of all its cells and then relocated into the nearest cell within 𝒜ℓ\mathcal{A}_{\ell} if it falls inside obstacle or unknown areas. After that, 𝒜ℓ\mathcal{A}_{\ell} is marked as exploring if it is adjacent to unknown area. Otherwise, it is marked as explored. The above process repeats to find all subareas {𝒜ℓ}ℓ=1L\{\mathcal{A}_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}. Fig. 2(b) shows an example where three disconnected subareas are identified. These subareas are then added as new nodes to the coverage guidance graph.

III-B Incremental Construction of Coverage Guidance Graph

A coverage guidance graph is incrementally built based on the detected subarea information, and used to track the search progress and compute the hierarchical coverage path.

Definition III.5 (Coverage Guidance Graph)

A coverage guidance graph 𝒢=(𝒩,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=\left(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{E}\right) is defined as an undirected complete graph that consists of:

  • •

    A node set 𝒩={nℓ:ℓ=0,…|𝒩|−1}\mathcal{N}=\left\{n_{\ell}:\ell=0,\ldots|\mathcal{N}|-1\right\}, where n0n_{0} represents robot’s current position pℛp_{\mathcal{R}} and the remaining node nℓn_{\ell} corresponds to a subarea 𝒜ℓ\mathcal{A}_{\ell} with center at pℓp_{\ell}.

  • •

    An edge set ℰ={eα:α=0,…|ℰ|−1}\mathcal{E}=\left\{e_{\alpha}:\alpha=0,\ldots\ |\mathcal{E}|-1\right\}, where each edge eα≡(ni,nj):ni≠nj,∀ni,nj∈𝒩e_{\alpha}\equiv\left(n_{i},n_{j}\right):n_{i}\neq n_{j},\forall n_{i},n_{j}\in\mathcal{N} represents the shortest collision-free path connecting two nodes computed by applying A∗ algorithm [21] on tiling 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Fig. 2 illustrates the process of incremental construction of the graph. It is first initialized with the node n0n_{0} and n1n_{1} which correspond to robot’s current position pℛp_{\mathcal{R}} and the current area 𝒜1\mathcal{A}_{1}, respectively. As seen in Fig. 2(a), the robot covers 𝒜1\mathcal{A}_{1} using greedy strategy. The environmental map reveals that 𝒜1\mathcal{A}_{1} is separated into three subareas, as shown in Fig. 2(b). Then, the graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} is updated by pruning current node with its edge and adding detected subareas as new nodes with associated edges as shown in Fig. 2(c). After that, a target node is selected from 𝒢\mathcal{G} for coverage. To track the coverage progress, each node of 𝒢\mathcal{G} is assigned a state using symbolic encoding Φ:𝒩→{C,O~,O^}\Phi:\mathcal{N}\rightarrow\{C,\widetilde{O},\hat{O}\}. While CC means that the node is already covered by the robot, O~\widetilde{O} (O^\hat{O}) means that the node is open for coverage and its corresponding subarea is exploring (explored). This encoding generates the set partition 𝒩={𝒩C,𝒩O~,𝒩O^}\mathcal{N}=\{\mathcal{N}_{C},\mathcal{N}_{\widetilde{O}},\mathcal{N}_{\hat{O}}\}. Next, a global coverage tour is computed to cover all nodes in 𝒩O~\mathcal{N}_{\widetilde{O}} and 𝒩O^\mathcal{N}_{\hat{O}} as described below.

III-C Global Coverage Tour Planning

To find an optimal tour to cover all open nodes starting from robot’s current position pℛp_{\mathcal{R}}, a modified TSP-based strategy is proposed. First, a complete undirected graph 𝒢¯=(𝒩¯,ℰ¯)\bar{\mathcal{G}}=(\bar{\mathcal{N}},\bar{\mathcal{E}}) is derived from 𝒩O~\mathcal{N}_{\widetilde{O}} and 𝒩O^\mathcal{N}_{\hat{O}} and consists of:

  • •

    A node set 𝒩¯={n¯i:n¯0≡pℛandn¯i∈𝒩∖𝒩C,∀i=1,…|𝒩¯|−1}\bar{\mathcal{N}}=\{\bar{n}_{i}:\bar{n}_{0}\equiv p_{\mathcal{R}}\ \textrm{and}\ \bar{n}_{i}\in\mathcal{N}\setminus\mathcal{N}_{C},\ \forall i=1,\ldots|\bar{\mathcal{N}}|-1\}, where pℛp_{\mathcal{R}} is robot’s current position.

  • •

    An edge set ℰ¯={e¯α:α=0,…|ℰ¯|−1}\bar{\mathcal{E}}=\left\{\bar{e}_{\alpha}:\alpha=0,\ldots|\bar{\mathcal{E}}|-1\right\}, where each edge e¯α≡(n¯i,n¯j):n¯i≠n¯j,∀n¯i,n¯j∈𝒩¯\bar{e}_{\alpha}\equiv\left(\bar{n}_{i},\bar{n}_{j}\right):\bar{n}_{i}\neq\bar{n}_{j},\forall\bar{n}_{i},\bar{n}_{j}\in\bar{\mathcal{N}} is assigned a cost wi​jw_{ij} equal to the shortest collision-free path length computed by applying A∗ algorithm [21] on tiling 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Then, the start node of TSP tour is set as the robot’s current position n¯0\bar{n}_{0} while the end node n¯β\bar{n}_{\beta} is determined as follows:

  • •

    Case 1: if 𝒩O~≠∅\mathcal{N}_{\widetilde{O}}\neq\emptyset, then its element that is furthest from n¯0\bar{n}_{0} is set as the end node. This allows for transition to the default greedy coverage strategy upon complete coverage of all explored nodes.

  • •

    Case 2: if 𝒩O~=∅\mathcal{N}_{\widetilde{O}}=\emptyset, then the end node is not specified.

Both cases aim to find an open-loop TSP tour starting from the robot’s current position and visiting all open nodes. To do this, a dummy node n¯𝒩¯\bar{n}_{\bar{\mathcal{N}}} is added to 𝒢¯\bar{\mathcal{G}} to convert this problem into a standard closed-loop TSP that starts and ends at the dummy node. The edge cost between n¯𝒩¯\bar{n}_{\bar{\mathcal{N}}} and n¯0\bar{n}_{0} is set as w𝒩¯,0=0w_{\bar{\mathcal{N}},0}=0. For case 1, the edge cost between n¯𝒩¯\bar{n}_{\bar{\mathcal{N}}} and the end node n¯β\bar{n}_{\beta} is set as w𝒩¯,β=0w_{\bar{\mathcal{N}},\beta}=0, while for case 2, it is set as w𝒩¯,β=∞w_{\bar{\mathcal{N}},\beta}=\infty. The edge costs between n¯𝒩¯\bar{n}_{\bar{\mathcal{N}}} and all the remaining nodes is set as w𝒩¯,i=∞,∀n¯i∈𝒩¯∖{n¯0,n¯β}w_{\bar{\mathcal{N}},i}=\infty,\forall\bar{n}_{i}\in\bar{\mathcal{N}}\setminus\{\bar{n}_{0},\bar{n}_{\beta}\}.

The cost matrix is obtained as 𝒲=[wi​j](𝒩¯+1)×(𝒩¯+1)\mathcal{W}=\left[w_{ij}\right]_{(\bar{\mathcal{N}}+1)\times(\bar{\mathcal{N}}+1)}. Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be the set of all Hamiltonian cycles corresponding to 𝒲\mathcal{W}. Each Hamiltonian cycle c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C} provides the order in which the nodes are visited and is expressed as follows:

c=(n(k)∈𝒩¯,k=0,…,𝒩¯+1:n(𝒩¯+1)=n(0)=n¯𝒩¯)c=\big(n(k)\in\bar{\mathcal{N}},k=0,\ldots,\bar{\mathcal{N}}+1:n(\bar{\mathcal{N}}+1)=n(0)=\bar{n}_{\bar{\mathcal{N}}}\big)

where n⁡(k)n(k) is the node visited at step kk, and n⁡(k)≠n⁡(k′)n(k)\neq n(k^{\prime}), k≠k′;∀k,k′=0,…,𝒩¯k\neq k^{\prime};\forall k,k^{\prime}=0,\ldots,\bar{\mathcal{N}}. The cost of a cycle cc is given as:

𝒥⁡(c)=∑k=0𝒩¯wn⁡(k)​n​(k+1)\mathcal{J}\left(c\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\bar{\mathcal{N}}}w_{n(k)n(k+1)}\vskip-5.0pt (2)

Then, the optimal Hamiltonian cycle c∗c^{*} is

c∗=argminc∈𝒞𝒥⁡(c)c^{*}=\mathop{\argmin}_{c\in\mathcal{C}}\mathcal{J}\left(c\right)\vskip-5.0pt (3)

The nearest neighbor algorithm [22] is used to obtain an initial cycle. Then, the 2-opt algorithm [22] is applied over this initial cycle to obtain the optimal solution c∗c^{*}. After that, the global coverage tour γg​l​o​b​a​l\gamma_{global} is obtained by removing the dummy node n¯𝒩¯\bar{n}_{\bar{\mathcal{N}}} and robot’s current position n¯0\bar{n}_{0} from c∗c^{*}. Fig. 2(c) shows an example of global coverage tour which covers two explored nodes and ends at the exploring node. The first element in γg​l​o​b​a​l\gamma_{global} is set as target node nt​a​r​g​e​tn_{target}.

III-D Local Coverage Path Planning

III-D1 Coverage of Exploring Node

As shown in Fig. 2(a), the robot covers exploring node by following greedy strategy which selects an uncovered cell as target τt​a​r​g​e​t\tau_{target} in the local vicinity based on the priority of movement direction {\{Left, Up, Down, Right}\}. These directions are defined with respect to the fixed global coordinate frame. The target cell τt​a​r​g​e​t\tau_{target} is marked as covered. This strategy generates the back-and-forth motions to completely cover target node nt​a​r​g​e​tn_{target}.

III-D2 Coverage of Explored Node

As shown in Fig. 2(d), the robot covers explored node by following the TSP-based optimal path. The start point of TSP tour is set as robot’s current position pℛp_{\mathcal{R}} while the end point is set as target cell τt​a​r​g​e​t\tau_{target}. To find an open-loop TSP tour to visit all cells of explored node, a dummy point is added. The cost between dummy point and pℛp_{\mathcal{R}} (and τt​a​r​g​e​t\tau_{target}) is set as 0 while the costs between dummy point and all cells is set as ∞\infty. The nearest neighbor algorithm [22] and 2-opt algorithm [22] are used to solve TSP for the local coverage path γl​o​c​a​l\gamma_{local}. Then, the robot follows this path to completely cover target node nt​a​r​g​e​tn_{target}.

III-E Time Complexity Analysis

The CAP algorithm is summarized in Algorithm 1. Since environmental map and robot’s position are updated continuously during navigation (Line 3), the complexity is evaluated for the steps of subarea identification (Line 5), graph construction (Line 7), global coverage tour planning (Line 8), and local coverage path planning (Line 15).

CAP recursively labels uncovered cells at most once to find all subareas. In the worst case, it searches the entire uncovered area 𝒯fu\mathcal{T}_{f}^{u} with O⁡(|𝒯fu|)O(|\mathcal{T}_{f}^{u}|) complexity. Next, the graph is updated as follows. First, the current node and associated edges are pruned as its corresponding area is separated into multiple parts {𝒜ℓ}ℓ=1L\{\mathcal{A}_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}. These identified subareas are added as new nodes to the graph with associated edges. In the worst case that the updated environmental map invalidates all old edges, A∗ algorithm is applied on 𝒯f\mathcal{T}_{f} to find new paths for all edges in ℰ\mathcal{E}, where |ℰ|=(|𝒩|2−|𝒩|)/2|\mathcal{E}|=(|\mathcal{N}|^{2}-|\mathcal{N}|)/2. Since A∗ algorithm has a complexity of O⁡(|𝒯f|2)O(|\mathcal{T}_{f}|^{2}) and |𝒯f|≫|𝒩||\mathcal{T}_{f}|\gg|\mathcal{N}|, the overall complexity of graph construction is O(|𝒯f|2|)O(|\mathcal{T}_{f}|^{2}|). After that, a TSP of size 𝒩¯+1\bar{\mathcal{N}}+1 is formulated and solved for the global coverage tour by the nearest neighbor algorithm and 2-opt algorithm with O⁡((𝒩¯+1)2)O(\left(\bar{\mathcal{N}}+1\right)^{2}) complexity [1]. Finally, the target node nt​a​r​g​e​tn_{target} is covered by using either greedy strategy with O⁡(1)O(1) complexity or TSP-based optimal path with O⁡(|nt​a​r​g​e​t|2)O(|n_{target}|^{2}) complexity. Since |𝒯f|≥|𝒯fu|≥|nt​a​r​g​e​t||\mathcal{T}_{f}|\geq|\mathcal{T}_{f}^{u}|\geq|n_{target}| and |𝒯f|≫|𝒩¯||\mathcal{T}_{f}|\gg|\bar{\mathcal{N}}|, the overall complexity of CAP is O⁡(|𝒯f|2)O(|\mathcal{T}_{f}|^{2}).

IV Results and Discussion

In this section, we present validation results of CAP comparing to five baseline algorithms.

IV-A Simulation Validations

The performance of CAP is first evaluated by extensive simulations on Gazebo (Fig. 3). As shown in Fig. 4, four complex scenes of dimensions 90​m×90​m90m\times 90m are generated with different obstacle layouts and partitioned into a 30×3030\times 30 tiling structure for mapping and coverage. Each scene depicts a real situation (e.g., office). A car-like robot is simulated with a maximum speed of 2​m/s2m/s and initialized at the bottom-left corner of the space. It is equipped with a lidar with a detection range of 12​m12m. Five baseline algorithms including ϵ∗\epsilon^{*} [12], BSA [8], BA∗ [11], BINN [9], and PPCPP [13] are selected for performance comparison in terms of coverage time, path length, and overlap ratio ⋃t∈[0,T]τ⁡(t)∖𝒯f𝒯f\frac{\bigcup_{t\in[0,T]}\tau(t)\setminus\mathcal{T}_{f}}{\mathcal{T}_{f}}.

Figs. 4(a)-4(d) show the coverage paths generated by different algorithms in four scenes. As seen, CAP provides complete coverage with less overlapping paths. This is because CAP constructs a coverage guidance graph to capture the global topological structure of the environment, and then computes a global tour on it to improve overall coverage efficiency and also address the issue of bypassing isolated regions. Additionally, it performs TSP-based optimal coverage path within the explored subareas to further minimize overlapping paths and local coverage time. In contrast, the baseline algorithms follow greedy strategies to achieve complete coverage without a global perspective of the entire search area, thus leading to highly overlapping paths and sub-optimal motions. Fig. 4(e) provides quantitative comparison results in terms of coverage time, path length, and overlap ratio. Overall, CAP achieves significant improvements over the baseline algorithms in all metrics. Particularly, in comparison to the second best baseline algorithm, CAP reduces coverage time by 21%,8%,15%,21\%,8\%,15\%, and 14%14\% in four scenes, respectively.

IV-B Real-World Experiments

The performance of CAP is also evaluated by two real-world experiments in a 60​m×24​m60m\times 24m warehouse space with different obstacle layouts (Fig. 3). The space is tiled with 2​m×2​m2m\times 2m cells. We utilize a Boston Dynamics Spot robot equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin and a Velodyne VLP-16 LiDAR. The robot is initialized at the bottom-left corner of the space. The LiPO [23] algorithm is used for localization and mapping. An overview of the autonomy stack for this robot is presented in [24]. Figs. 5 and 6 show the coverage paths generated by different algorithms in both the real-world experiments. CAP provides complete coverage with less overlapping paths. As shown in Fig. 7, CAP provides a superior solution quality in all metrics. Particularly, in comparison to the second best baseline algorithm, CAP reduces coverage time by 15%15\% and 9%9\% in two experiments.

V Conclusions and Future Work

In this paper, we present CAP algorithm for efficient coverage path planning of unknown environments. During online operation, a coverage guidance graph is incrementally built to capture essential environmental information. Then, a hierarchical coverage path is computed on the graph to improve global coverage efficiency and minimize local coverage time. CAP is comparatively evaluated by high-fidelity simulations and real-world experiments. The results show that CAP yields significant improvements in coverage time, path length, and path overlap ratio. Future works include multi-robot coverage with communication limits, coverage of 3D terrain, and coverage of dynamic environments [25].

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
